project_name: Reliable Surrogate Models of Noisy Data
summary: This project, awarded first place, asked how reliably BO reaches an optimum when the objective is noisy, and whether encoding a noise assumption into the surrogate helps. The team used the two-dimensional Schwefel function---highly multimodal, with its global minimum geometrically distant from the next-best basins---with additive Gaussian noise, and swept a grid of noise standard deviations (1, 5, 10, 20) and initial design sizes (2, 4, 8, 10) over a 30-evaluation budget with five random seeds. In the BoTorch arm\cite{balandat2020botorch}, a Gaussian-process surrogate that infers a homoscedastic noise level was compared against the same model with the observation variance pinned to a near-zero constant, scoring each run by the best noise-free function value found. The noise-aware model won in 15 of the 16 grid cells, and its margin grew with noise: negligible at the lowest noise level but 6.6 to 26.5 objective units at the highest. The BayBE arm\cite{fitzner2022baybe} ran greedy expected-improvement campaigns against a random-recommender baseline over both a restricted range and the wider domain containing the global optimum; there, the team observed that most campaigns settled into local minima far from the global optimum while some high-noise and random runs found the global basin early, so BO's advantage over random search was not robust at this budget. Their conclusion was that a noise-aware surrogate matters more the noisier the data, but no surrogate rescues a budget too small for the landscape. (No recorded video was submitted for this project; this summary was prepared from the team's project page and the notebooks, scripts and result figures in their code repository.)
